adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: National-framework document for West Nusa Tenggara: Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, and in December 2022 Parliament passed a new Penal Code that criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison and complaints admissible from immediate family, a provision set to take effect on 2 January 2026 - the code the record's first claim references. The page also records that in Aceh homosexuality is illegal under sharia law with flogging or imprisonment, that police raids on 'gay parties' continue (75 people arrested at a private villa near Jakarta on 22 June 2025, plus raids in South Jakarta in February and May 2025), that conversion therapy is widely practiced, and that 93% of Indonesians labelled homosexuality 'morally unacceptable' in Pew data cited for 2025. It does not name West Nusa Tenggara specifically; it is the encompassing national framework under which the province stands.

adds.title: West Nusa Tenggara - Wikipedia
adds.summary: The province's own page: West Nusa Tenggara consists of the two large islands of Lombok and Sumbawa, has an estimated population of 5,731,110 (mid-2025 official estimate), and is overwhelmingly Muslim - 96.88% per 2022 Ministry of Religious Affairs data - with Islam documented as the official religion of the region's historical kings. The majority Sasak people of Lombok preserve strong traditions ('Wetu Telu', a form of Islam influenced by local beliefs), and the page stresses the provinces' conservative religious character and tourism-dependent economy. It contains no LGBT-specific statute or incident, but it documents the demographic and cultural setting - the record's 'Lombok culture' claim - in which the province's LGBT-related bylaws and the national Penal Code's morality provisions operate.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Mexico - Wikipedia
adds.summary: The national framework page names Yucatán directly: on 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners were able to marry and on 8 August 2013 the first same-sex couple legally married in the state; the Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015 and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022, and Yucatán is listed as enacting a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, still in effect alongside the state bans from Mexico City (31 July 2020) and elsewhere. The page also records the federal framework: same-sex acts decriminalised since 1871, tolerance of sexual diversity documented among Yucatán Maya groups, and the conversion-therapy ban passed federally by the Chamber of Deputies in March 2023 (267-104) after a 69-16 Senate vote in October 2022.

adds.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: HRW's state-by-state rundown of legal gender recognition (March 2025) carries a dedicated Yucatán entry: 'In 2024, the state's congress passed a reform to the Civil Registry Law to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition', linking to the state's official gazette (Diario Oficial, 26 April 2024, on yucatan.gob.mx). This places Yucatán among the Mexican states with an administrative - rather than court-ordered - route for transgender people to update legal gender, which is the concrete local procedure a trans visitor's document situation turns on; the same feature explains which states lack any procedure.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
adds.summary: National-framework document for Kwara State: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, signed in January 2014, voids same-sex unions and criminalises forming, operating or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations, and up to 14 years' imprisonment applies to same-sex sexual activity under federal law (Criminal Code in the south, Penal Code in the north). The page names the twelve states it says have adopted sharia law - Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara - and Kwara is not among them, so this source supplies the federal framework under which Kwara stands but does not itself document the Ilorin-area sharia penal application the record alleges. It also records the 2022 court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the SSMPA are unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide.

adds.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's report on the SSMPA's impact records that the 2014 law carries 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations and bans same-sex cohabitation and public shows of same-sex amorous relationships, and that its passage was followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions of LGBT people across the country, including 21 young men arrested but never charged at an Ibadan birthday gathering. The report is national in scope and names no Kwara-specific case, but it substantiates the federal criminalisation and arbitrary-enforcement climate on which Kwara's visitor assessment rests, complementing the record's claims about the federal SSMPA framework.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
adds.summary: National-framework document for Rivers State: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, makes same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal and criminalises registering, operating or supporting gay organisations, while the Nigerian Criminal Code in the south criminalises sex between men with penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years. The page records that in 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists sued over Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act and the court ruled them unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, effectively allowing LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise freely, but notes there are no legal protections for LGBTQ people and that sharia-based states apply penalties from lashing up to death. The page does not name Rivers or Port Harcourt specifically; it supplies the federal framework the state's visitors stand under.

adds.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the SSMPA (passed January 2014) records that the law imposes 10 to 14 years' imprisonment on anyone who registers, operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. It documents that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after the Act, including eight of the 21 young men arrested, but never charged, at a birthday party in Ibadan, and - relevant to Rivers State itself - the case of Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos who in January 2015 travelled to Port Harcourt to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there, saying he did not report it to the police. The named Port Harcourt incident and the nationwide abuse pattern substantiate the enforcement climate a same-sex couple or trans visitor faces in Rivers.
